source: Before the Action: Benchmarking LLMs on Prospective Hypothesis Discovery (HypoArena), re-read for gap 4
finding: Agent mode is a pipeline of skills chosen from a library of 12, ACH being one. The paper reports no per-skill ablation, no count of how often ACH was picked, and no token cost. So the -60 to +88 spread cannot be assigned to ACH.
numbers: 15 models; 988 cases in 6 domains; per-model change Agent minus Baseline from +88 (kimi-k2.5) to about -60 (claude-opus-4.6; figure label -58); Spearman rho -0.10 with baseline strength; 1,500 human pairwise checks, Kendall tau 0.90.
quote: structured analytic skills act as a model-dependent intervention, with candidate compression as one observed failure mode
limits: Judge is an LLM (seed-2.0-pro) with a second judge as check. Compression is seen in 'several inspected traces', not measured. Gap 4 stays open for the ACH share.
agent_relevance: Do not read HypoArena as evidence for or against a matrix step. It is evidence that a long multi-skill pipeline can lose breadth at the final write-up.

source: HypoArena Appendix E and K: candidate compression and the 12-skill library
finding: Appendix E names a failure mode: systems build rich intermediate analysis, then squeeze it into a narrow final set and drop plausible candidates. This is worst under Agent Mode. The skill list includes ACH (C/I/NA scoring, rank by least disconfirming evidence) and a separate Diagnostic Reasoning skill that only picks the highest-diagnostic evidence.
numbers: 12 skills incl. ACH, Chronology, Assumptions Check, Brainstorming, Cross-Impact, Devil's Advocacy, Diagnostic Reasoning, Morphological, Premortem, Red Hat, Starbursting, What-If. Contexts average about 3,000 tokens; hypothesis-evidence pairs about 1,000 tokens.
quote: These systems identify multiple plausible lines of reasoning internally yet fail to preserve them in the submitted set.
limits: Compression is qualitative. Because diagnosticity is its own skill, a diagnosticity-only arm exists in the library but was not run alone.
agent_relevance: A matrix step needs a rule to carry all live hypotheses into the final answer. Without it the narrowing at the end can undo the breadth. Test: count hypotheses kept before and after the final write-up.

source: Filbry, Melo, Gal (2026) From Prompts to Posteriors: Can LLM Agents Perform Bayesian Inference in Context? - coherence part
finding: When probabilities are asked in separate chats, LLM judgments often break basic probability rules. When asked inside one dialogue, violations drop sharply. So incoherence mostly comes from having no shared record of earlier answers.
numbers: Dutch-book test on 30 forecasting scenarios, 3 models. Across chats: violation rates above 50% of scenarios for almost all model-by-axiom pairs. Within one dialogue: 10% for Gemini-2.5-Pro and 1 of 30 scenarios for Gemma-4-31B.
quote: cross-conversation incoherence reflects the absence of a persistent common representation rather than an inability to apply elementary probability rules
limits: Only 3 models and 30 scenarios. Does not test matrix prompts. Human ACH users were incoherent within one sitting (K05), so the LLM and human patterns differ.
agent_relevance: A visible running belief state in context (a table that holds all hypothesis probabilities at once) is what gives coherence. This supports keeping one joint belief table, not a separate matrix ritual.

source: Filbry et al. (2026) - accuracy of in-context Bayesian updating, no reasoning vs reasoning
finding: Without reasoning, LLMs miss the Bayes posterior and lose a lot of downstream success. With native reasoning, the best open model matched the oracle on simple tasks for up to 10 pieces of evidence. Errors left were numeric slips, not wrong logic.
numbers: Non-reasoning: final success lower by at least 30% versus the oracle in both environments, near 0% accuracy for weaker models on 20 Questions. Reasoning: Gemma-4-31B-it matched oracle across the whole ProteinWorld-simple run; consistent updates up to 10 experiments.
quote: errors stem from numerical slips rather than conceptual failures
limits: Evidence units are tests with known likelihoods, not text cues. Not an ACH test. Models are open-weight reasoning models; the thinking switch is the variable.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 5, partial: a thinking model can combine independent evidence well without any matrix. The matrix is not what supplies the arithmetic. Gap 5 (correlated cues) is not covered: the likelihoods were conditionally independent by design.

source: Filbry et al. (2026) - code execution and the BED-LLM harness comparison
finding: With code tools, a model approximated a posterior with no closed form. A heavy structured harness (BED-LLM, ICLR 2026) no longer beat a plain in-context prompt on current reasoning models. The harness helped older models.
numbers: ProteinWorld-hard: reasoning plus code gave KL and mass gap near 0; reasoning alone did not. 20Q: naive baseline with reasoning matched BED-LLM across the discovery process and exceeded it in parts (3 open-source reasoning models).
quote: the appropriate division of labor between the LLM and its surrounding harness is a moving target
limits: Figure-level result; no table of numbers or confidence intervals was given. 20 Questions only.
agent_relevance: Direct support for schema 4b: a structure that helps a weak model can become dead weight for a reasoning model. Re-test any added step on the target model.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) Dutch Books for Language Models - baseline incoherence
finding: LLM probability forecasts are incoherent under single-question elicitation. The measure is the largest guaranteed arbitrage profit per unit stake. Coherence differs between models far more than accuracy does.
numbers: GPT-OSS-120B, 100 stock-days, 14 events each: mean profit 0.002067 (95% CI 0.001471 to 0.002737); at least 0.1% in 48 of 100, at least 0.5% in 15, at least 1% in 6. 15 models: profit from 0.002067 to 0.1994 (about 100x), Brier only 0.1966 to 0.2157; Spearman 0.9143; 101 of 105 pairwise profit differences exclude zero versus 32 for Brier.
limits: Stock-return bins, not intelligence cues. Only one workhorse model has 5 passes; the 14 others ran one pass. Possible lookahead bias for models released after the sample.
agent_relevance: Coherence is measurable without ground truth. It can be a cheap label-free check inside the agent: ask the same question in complement form and compare.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) - joint elicitation of the full event panel
finding: Asking about the whole set of related events in ONE query drives incoherence to about the rounding floor. Asking about unrelated pairs raises it. This is the closest LLM analogue to filling a matrix row-by-row versus all cells at once.
numbers: Full panel of 14 next-day events in one query: incoherence near zero (same order as the 5e-5 rounding limit). Complement pairs: significant decrease. Relation-poor pairs: significant increase.
limits: One model (GPT-OSS-120B) and one event structure. The authors say users will not normally ask this way.
agent_relevance: Gap 6, partial. Coherence repair for an LLM can come from a single joint elicitation step, not from many samples. Cheap in tokens: one call instead of K.

source: Andrews and Sarkar (2026) - averaging samples and irrelevant context
finding: Averaging up to 5 repeated answers lowers incoherence only a little, because 95% of answers were identical across all 5 passes. Adding irrelevant context (a feeling, a gut number, a phone battery figure) raises incoherence, by up to an order of magnitude overall.
numbers: Averaging 1 to 5 passes: gains 'modest'. Identical answers across 5 passes: 95%. Headline and instruction arms: large significant increases; a statistics arm: significant decrease.
quote: adding more information to the prompt may hurt coherence
limits: Low answer variance of one model limits what averaging can do. Temperature 1 was set where the provider allowed it.
agent_relevance: Gap 6: the human gain from pooling 50 analysts (MAE .23 to .09) does not carry to small groups of same-model samples, since samples barely differ. Diversity must come from different prompts or models (see d10).

source: Shen and Yao (2026) Not All Test-Time Compute Is Evidence: Model-Specific Bias in LLM Reasoning - correlated errors
finding: Repeated samples from one reasoning model make correlated errors. When the majority vote is wrong, the wrong samples often collapse onto one answer. Full CoT often keeps the first wrong answer. Self-selection prefers the final stage.
numbers: Self-selection on reasoning-stage disagreements (Qwen3-8B): picks the final-stage answer 97.7% (MuSR) and 95.1% (MMLU-Pro); selection accuracy 44.1% and 63.4%. Error concentration grows with model scale (SC@20, MMLU-Pro, GPQA-Diamond).
quote: more compute from the same model is not more evidence
limits: Preprint. Mostly figures; the scale trend is read from plots.
agent_relevance: Gap 5 and 6, partial. Same-model repeated samples are the LLM version of double counting: they look like many votes but carry one vote of information. A matrix of rows produced by one pass has the same problem.

source: Shen and Yao (2026) - heterogeneous independent solvers, ablations and token cost
finding: A trigger-and-arbitrate scheme (DIA) with three different external models beat full CoT in 12 of 14 settings while firing on 17% of items and using up to 47.2% fewer tokens than a multi-agent baseline. Replacing the heterogeneous panel with three samples of the base model cut arbitration accuracy sharply.
numbers: MuSiQue +7.00% over CoT. Homogeneous vs heterogeneous panel: MuSR 51.16 vs 55.81 (-4.65); 2WikiMultiHopQA 19.23 vs 53.85 (-34.62); MuSiQue 24.53 vs 54.72 (-30.19). Full-trace comparison picks the final answer 93.0% (MuSR) and 91.8% (MMLU-Pro) of the time. Scaling Qwen3-8B/30B/80B on MuSR: CoT 60.00/62.00/66.00, DIA 63.50/66.00/68.50.
limits: Table text extracted from the PDF is partly garbled; column pairing is read by position. Needs outside models, so it is not a single-agent method.
agent_relevance: Gap 6 at equal cost: for a single agent, diversity is the lever, not count. Trace comparison by the same model does not repair errors (the judge sees the final answer as better).

source: Jhaveri, GX-Chen, Sucholutsky, Choi (2026) Failing to Falsify: confirmation bias in language models - base results
finding: Eleven LLMs show confirmation bias in a Wason 2-4-6 style rule game. The share of disconfirming tests (I:C ratio) correlates positively with success, in thinking and non-thinking modes.
numbers: 11 model scenarios; 80 episodes per model-variant; significant positive I:C vs success correlation in both modes, stronger for thinking models. Thinking mode raised success without raising I:C consistently.
limits: Abstract numbers are averages over models. Task is rule discovery on integer triples, not evidence evaluation.
agent_relevance: Supports a disconfirm-first guardrail. It also shows the gain from thinking mode is not from less confirmation bias.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) - Think-in-Opposites and Dual-Goal prompts, thinking vs non-thinking
finding: Think-in-Opposites (propose a test that would break your hypothesis) improved task success in all 11 model scenarios. Dual-Goal (hold two rules) improved 8 of 11 and slightly hurt non-thinking models. Gains were significant only for thinking models. Cost: thinking models use about 1,000 to 2,300 tokens per turn versus about 6 to 24 for non-thinking.
numbers: Average rule discovery 42% to 56% with interventions. TiO better in 11 of 11; Dual-Goal better in 8 of 11; I:C up in 18 of 22 cases. Distilling TiO behaviour 'almost tripled' success for one student setup and transferred to a Blicket test.
limits: Never compared with a full ACH matrix, so gap 7 (cheap disconfirm rule vs full ACH) is not answered head to head. Tokens per turn rise under TiO for several thinking models.
agent_relevance: A one-line disconfirm-first prompt has measured gains on LLMs. The matrix has none. Keep the one-liner and gate it on thinking-capable models.

source: Adversary Brains: Hypothesis-Based Logical Signatures for Threat Actor Detection with LLMs (2026)
finding: A design paper that runs ACH by machine, with each hypothesis as a scored 'brain' updated as observations arrive. It reports no accuracy test against a plain baseline.
numbers: No accuracy numbers and no baseline arm found in the text.
limits: Design and wager paper; the author describes a plan to test the wager.
agent_relevance: Another untested ACH-by-LLM system. Adds to K16 (no measured benefit).

source: arXiv listing sweep for gaps 1, 2, 5, 8, 10 (queries run 2026-11-03)
finding: Searches for ACH with LLMs (21 hits), intelligence analysis plus LLM (15 hits), structured analytic techniques (0 hits), analytic techniques plus language model (24 hits), confirmation bias plus language models, anchoring bias mitigation, and forecasting tournament plus structured analytic found NO paper that compares an ACH matrix prompt against a plain prompt on one model, none that tests diagnosticity ratings alone, none that tests double counting of correlated cues, and none that tests ACH as an anchoring or order-effect debiasing prompt.
numbers: Hits that touch ACH: HypoArena (2607.15766), AgentCDM (2508.11995), PRISM, Adversary Brains (2610.35624); related but not ACH: SIA (2606.13220), EviDx (2608.24570, no hypothesis-tracking ablation found).
limits: arXiv search is all-terms; rate limits blocked the arXiv API, Semantic Scholar and OpenAlex today, and the WebSearch quota was used up. A miss here is weak evidence of absence. Journal-only papers (Taylor and Francis, RAND, MITRE) were not reachable (HTTP 403).
agent_relevance: As of 2026-11-03 gaps 1, 2, 5 and 10 look empty in the public preprint literature. They are open questions we would have to run ourselves.

source: Computed check of PRISM's ACH stage (+0.8) against sampling noise, from the saved PRISM text (Lee, Kang, Shin 2026)
finding: PRISM ran one deterministic pass (temperature 0) on 250 MuSR murder questions for each of 10 models, and gives no interval. +0.8 points equals about 2 questions per model. A rough unpaired standard error for a difference of two accuracies near 70% over 2,500 model-item runs is about 1.3 points, so +0.8 is inside one standard error. The paired SE is smaller but is not reported.
numbers: 250 questions, 10 models; Direct 58.1, CoT 57.2, PRISM 71.3; ACH step 70.5 to 71.3 (+0.8). My own SE: sqrt(2*0.7*0.3/2500) = 0.013. Limitations section: only MuSR tested.
quote: experiments were conducted on the MuSR murder mystery benchmark
limits: The SE is my arithmetic, not a result from the paper. Gap 3 (other tasks) stays open: no other task is tested.
agent_relevance: Treat the ACH stage as not distinguishable from zero in PRISM. Do not credit ACH for the PRISM gain.
